observation_summary: The Mockito framework fails to correctly handle polymorphic calls when an interface (like Iterable) is extended by another interface (like MyIterable) and then mocked. Stubbing and verification on the base interface (Iterable) fail when called through the sub-interface mock.
hypothesis: The root cause is an algorithmic flaw in how Mockito identifies and matches methods on mocked objects when dealing with bridge methods or polymorphic interface inheritance. The framework fails to correctly map the method call on the base interface to the stubbed method on the sub-interface.
prediction: The fix will involve updating the method lookup or invocation matching algorithm within Mockito to correctly account for bridge methods or inherited generic methods, ensuring that calls to base interface methods are correctly routed to the stubbed implementation.
experiment_rationale: The failure occurs specifically when casting a mock of a sub-interface to its base interface and calling a method defined in the base interface. This indicates that the internal mechanism responsible for matching method signatures is not correctly resolving the inheritance hierarchy or bridge methods generated by the compiler.
reasoning_summary: The issue is not a missing check (Checking), a wrong value (Assignment/Initialization), or a design-level capability gap (Function/Class/Object). It is a failure in the internal procedure that matches method invocations to stubbed methods, which is a core algorithmic task in a mocking framework. Therefore, Algorithm/Method is the most appropriate classification.
evidence_gaps: The internal implementation of the method matching algorithm is not provided in the snippets, only the test case demonstrating the failure.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the issue involves interface inheritance, the failure is in the internal logic of the mocking framework (matching the call to the stub), not a mismatch in the interface contract itself.
The capability to mock interfaces exists; the issue is a bug in the implementation of the method matching logic, not a missing design capability.
